cues.text: A Princess Sent Away as a Child

Born in 1207, the daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary and Queen Gertrude, Elizabeth was betrothed in infancy, according to the political customs of the age, to Landgrave Hermann I of Thuringia’s eldest son.
At only four years old, she was sent five hundred miles from her Hungarian homeland to be raised at the Thuringian court, where her future marriage would eventually take place.
She arrived as a small child among strangers, in a language and land not her own.
Tragedy struck early: Elizabeth's mother was murdered by Hungarian nobles in 1213.
The intended bridegroom himself died a few years later, after which Elizabeth was instead betrothed to his younger brother, Ludwig .
Against the usual pattern of such arranged medieval unions, the match grew into a marriage of genuine and deep mutual affection.
A Marriage of Real Devotion
Elizabeth and Ludwig were married in 1221 and, by the consistent testimony of contemporaries, shared a marriage marked by real love and mutual support.
Far from suppressing his young wife's growing devotion to prayer, penance, and care for the poor, Ludwig actively protected and encouraged her charitable impulses.

These habits made her something of a curiosity, and occasionally a target of mockery, among the more worldly members of the Thuringian court; even, tradition holds, he knelt beside her at night as she prayed.
Charity in a Time of Crisis
In 1226, while Ludwig was away attending to political affairs, floods and disease struck Thuringia.
Elizabeth took charge of the crisis response in her husband's absence, distributing alms across the territory without restraint.
She even gave away state robes and ceremonial ornaments to relieve the suffering she found.

She personally built a hospital of twenty-eight beds below the family castle, where she nursed the sick with her own hands, work considered remarkably undignified for a woman of her rank in the medieval imagination.
Widowed and Cast Out
In 1227, Ludwig set out to join the crusading army being assembled by Emperor Frederick II.
He died of illness before ever reaching the Holy Land, leaving Elizabeth, still only twenty years old, a widow with three young children.

In the political upheaval that followed, Elizabeth was effectively expelled from the Wartburg castle by relatives unwilling to support a widowed landgravine and her children, reduced almost overnight from a position of real power to genuine homelessness and hardship.
A Life Given Entirely to the Poor

Rather than seek the security of a new advantageous marriage, an option readily available to a woman of her rank and connections, Elizabeth chose instead to embrace even more completely the life of radical charity she had already begun.
Influenced by the newly arrived Franciscan friars and their ideal of Gospel poverty, she used what remained of her resources to found a hospital at Marburg .
There, she personally nursed the sick, the elderly, and the dying, embracing a life of severe simplicity.
Her own confessor at times urged her, without success, to moderate it.
Legacy
Elizabeth died at Marburg on November 17, 1231, worn out by illness and the physical demands of her ceaseless charity, only twenty-four years old.
Her reputation for holiness was so immediate and so widespread that she was canonized just four years later, in 1235 — an extraordinarily rapid recognition even by the standards of her era.
Patron of Catholic charities, hospitals, and the homeless, Elizabeth remains one of the medieval Church's most vivid and enduring images.
Her life shows what royal privilege, entirely surrendered to the service of the poor, can accomplish within a life that, however brief, was never once wasted.
Fewer than a quarter century on this earth, and yet centuries of hospitals and charities still quietly bear the shape of what she began.
